catalog_locator: Westermann & Bryan 1952, p. 134, 'Linguistic notes on IBIBIO-EFIK', note 3 with fn. 2 (archive.org languagesofwesta0000west, search-inside fragments); Cook 1969 in Dunstan (ed.), ch. 3, sec. IV 'Tone, intonation and stress': heading and point 1 on p. 42, point 5 (the stress sentence) on p. 43 (archive.org twelvenigerianla0000duns, search-inside fragments). Drop 'leaf 226' and 'leaf 202': they are not the leaves of these pages.
catalog_quote: 3. There are two basic tone levels, high and low. Falling and rising tones also occur. A mid, or lowered high, tone is found, as a lexical tone, after another high tone in some Nouns, and also occurs in certain grammatical constructions. Stress is of secondary importance. Stressing of the Root syllable has been observed.2 [fn.] 2 I. C. Ward, The phonetic and tonal structure of Efik, p. 29. ... [Cook in Dunstan 1969, p. 42] IV TONE, INTONATION AND STRESS 1 Efik is a terraced-level tone language. ... 5 Not all syllables in Efik are pronounced with the same degree of stress. No satisfactory analysis of stress has yet been made, however.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Efik is a tone language (H, L, contour tones, lowered-high/downstep); stress is not a primary (contrastive) feature, but such prominence as exists falls on the root syllable (i.e. the stem/root rather than prefixes), per Ward's 1933 observation relayed by the handbook.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the statement is hedged ('has been observed').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remark in a handbook thumbnail sketch; no discussion of phrase vs citation forms. The note is headed IBIBIO-EFIK but the tone/stress sentences rest on Ward's description of Calabar Efik.
new_statements.identity_note: Westermann & Bryan's note is headed 'IBIBIO-EFIK' (their dialect cluster) but the tone/stress sentences are explicitly about EFIK and footnoted to Ward 1933, a description of Calabar (Creek Town/Duke Town) Efik = efik1245; Ibibio proper is ibib1240.

tone.quote: Second, Efik is a tonal language in which lexical and grammatical contrasts are encoded through pitch variation [11]. Accurate synthesis therefore requires careful modeling of tonal contours in addition to segmental phonetic structure. Inadequate tone realization can alter lexical meaning, reducing intelligibility and perceived naturalness.
